extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, practitioners, and USPTO examiners involved in filing or processing Hague (international) design applications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural/substantive standards for preparing, filing (directly or indirectly), and prosecuting international design applications under the Hague Agreement, with emphasis on filings designating the United States and USPTO processing as an office of indirect filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to file (Article 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person that is a national of a Contracting Party or of a State member of an intergovernmental organization that is a Contracting Party, or that has a domicile, a habitual residence, or a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in the territory of a Contracting Party, shall be entitled to file an international application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be entitled to file an international design application, a person must: (1) be a national of a Contracting Party or of a State that is a member of an intergovernmental organization that is a Contracting Party; or (2) have a domicile, habitual residence, or real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in the territory of a Contracting Party. Article 1(ix) defines “person” and Article 1(xiii) defines “Contracting Party.” See WIPO member list for Contracting Parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s Contracting Party must be identified
rubrics_metrics.description: The international application must indicate the applicant’s Contracting Party (the Contracting Party from which the applicant derives entitlement to file under Article 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 1(xiv) defines the applicant’s Contracting Party. If more than one Contracting Party could provide entitlement, the applicant must expressly identify which is the applicant’s Contracting Party in the international design application (DM/1 form includes boxes for entitlement and applicant’s Contracting Party). For filing through the USPTO as office of indirect filing, the United States must be applicant’s Contracting Party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing method: direct or indirect (Article 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international design application may be filed either directly with the International Bureau or indirectly through the Office of the applicant’s Contracting Party; Contracting Parties may declare that applications may not be filed indirectly through their office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct filing with IB (e.g., eHague) or indirect filing via an Office are options. The WIPO website provides which Contracting Parties permit indirect filing. Indirect filing may require a transmittal fee to the Office used for filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to file through USPTO as office of indirect filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Only persons who are nationals of the United States or who have a domicile, a habitual residence, or a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in the territory of the United States may file international design applications through the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 35 U.S.C. 382(a) and 37 C.F.R. 1.1011(a). Additionally, to file through the USPTO the United States must be the applicant’s Contracting Party (37 C.F.R. 1.1012). The USPTO may refuse designation if the applicant is not qualified under 35 U.S.C. chapter 11 to be an applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmittal fee and national security clearance for USPTO-filed applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment of the transmittal fee and satisfaction of national security review/clearance are required before the USPTO will transmit an international design application to the International Bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application will not be transmitted to the International Bureau if the transmittal fee has not been paid, necessary national security clearance has not been obtained, or required entitlement indications are absent. If conditions are not met the USPTO will notify the applicant by Form PTO-2320. See 35 U.S.C. 382(b), 37 C.F.R. 1.1045 and § 1.1031(a) for transmittal fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO review on receipt (entitlement, fees, security)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt the USPTO will confirm required transmittal fee payment, perform a security review, and check that required indications demonstrating entitlement to file through the USPTO are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If indications are insufficient, fee not paid, or security clearance missing the Office will notify applicant via Form PTO-2320. An application not transmitted to IB within six months of USPTO receipt may receive an IB filing date different than the USPTO receipt date (subject to Rule 14(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date rules — international vs. USPTO filing date (Article 9; Rules 13–14)
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Bureau accords the international filing date; for applications filed indirectly the filing date may be the Office receipt date provided IB receives the application within prescribed time periods; certain irregularities can postpone the filing date until corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where filed directly, filing date is when IB receives the application (subject to corrections). Where filed through an Office, if governed exclusively by the 1999 Act the Office receipt date counts if IB receives the application within one month (or six months where security clearance period applies). Irregularities that entail postponement are listed in Rule 14(2) (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required elements for accorded filing date (Rule 14(2) / Rule 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: The international application must be in one of the prescribed languages (English, French, Spanish) and must include: (1) an indication that international registration is sought; (2) indications allowing identity of the applicant to be established; (3) indications sufficient to enable the applicant or representative to be contacted; (4) a reproduction or specimen of each industrial design that is the subject of the application; and (5) the designation of at least one Contracting Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these elements are missing at the time IB receives the application, the filing date is the date on which the missing element is received by the IB. See Hague Rule 6 (languages) and Rule 13/14 for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularities and time limits to correct (Rule 14(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: If IB finds the application does not fulfill applicable requirements it will invite the applicant to make required corrections within three months (or two months for fee shortfalls), failing which the application may be considered abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 14(1)(a) — three months from invitation to correct; Rule 14(1)(b) — where fees received are less than the basic fee for one design IB may invite payment of at least the basic fee within two months. Failure to timely respond can result in abandonment and refund (after deduction) per Rule 14(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language requirement (Rule 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The international application shall be in English, French, or Spanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuant to Rule 6, the IB will accord a filing date only if the application is in a prescribed language. If not, correction is required and filing date may be postponed until correction is received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and deferment options
rubrics_metrics.description: International registrations are published by the International Bureau; applicants may request immediate publication or defer publication (subject to limitations) for up to 30 months from the filing or priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deferment is not possible if a designated Contracting Party does not permit deferred publication; for applications filed on/after 1 Jan 2022 absent a request the registration will be published 12 months after international registration (earlier rules produced 6-month default). The publication includes International Register data and reproductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: US-specific non-deferment of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the United States is designated in an international design application, it is not possible for an applicant to request the deferment of publication of the ensuing international registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a U.S. declaration pursuant to Article 11(1)(b) and Rule 11(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: One independent and distinct design per application (Article 13(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one independent and distinct design may be claimed in a single application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuant to Article 13(1) and U.S. declarations; see MPEP §§ 2920.05(b) and 1504.05 for related examination guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim wording requirement for U.S. designation (Article 5(2)(a) / Rule 11(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: An international design application designating the United States must contain a claim, and the specific wording of the claim shall be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article as shown, or as shown and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. 1.1021(d) and MPEP § 2909 subsection IV. The formal claim wording requirement is a U.S. declaration under Article 5(2)(a) and Rule 11(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath or declaration of creator required for U.S. designation (Rule 8(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: An international design application designating the United States must contain an oath or declaration of the creator and indications concerning the identity of the creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is required by U.S. declaration pursuant to Rule 8(1). See MPEP § 2909 and 37 C.F.R. provisions addressing inventor’s oath/declaration for design applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part individual designation fee and timing (Article 7(2), Rule 12(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The prescribed designation fee is replaced by an individual designation fee payable in two parts: a first part at filing and a second part payable upon allowance of the application (for certain designated Offices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. declared replacement of designation fee by two-part fee; amounts of first and second parts are subject to change. Where Rule 12(3) applies, grant of protection may be subject to payment of the second part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claims inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The international registration includes any priority claim where the earlier filing is not more than six months prior to the international filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority documents and related requirements for designated Contracting Parties may be triggered by publication or other dates; applicants should consult WIPO Hague Member Profiles for specific countries' requirements for priority documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination by designated Contracting Parties (substantive examination variability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following IB publication, offices of designated Contracting Parties may proceed with substantive examination if required by their laws; some do not examine, some examine on limited grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The International Bureau’s Hague Member Profiles database provides details on the scope of substantive examination by designated Contracting Parties. If a designated office notifies refusal, IB transmits the refusal to the holder; replies must be communicated directly to that office.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. examination and notification of refusal timing (35 U.S.C. 389)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO will examine international design applications designating the United States based on the published international registration; where it appears the applicant is not entitled to a patent, the Office will send a notification of refusal normally within 12 months from publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may reply directly to the USPTO. Further Office actions (non-final rejection, final rejection, allowance) will be sent directly to the applicant. U.S. has declared extension of refusal period to 12 months under Rule 18(1)(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of international registration as grant of protection (Article 14(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 14(2) provides that international registration shall have the same effect as a grant of protection under the law of a Contracting Party at the latest from the date of expiration of the period allowed to communicate a refusal, but national laws may specify different effects and timings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the United States, a grant of protection for an industrial design that is the subject of an international registration arises only through issuance of a U.S. patent (37 C.F.R. 1.1071 and 35 U.S.C. 389(d) / 171). The Hague Agreement is not self-executing in the U.S. with respect to conferment of patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term/duration of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracting Parties must provide a minimum period of protection of 15 years counted from the international registration date, but the United States provides a term of 15 years from date of grant for U.S. design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration and renewal rules vary among Contracting Parties; many require renewals at five-year increments. For the U.S., 35 U.S.C. 173 sets term at 15 years from grant; renewal fees to maintain international registration are not required to maintain a U.S. patent issued on an international design application (37 C.F.R. 1.1031(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording changes and effects in International Register (Article 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Bureau records specified changes (change in ownership, name/address of holder, appointment of representative, renunciation, limitation, invalidation, other facts) in the International Register; recording may have effects in Contracting Parties unless a Contracting Party declared otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Contracting Party may declare that certain recordings (e.g., change in ownership) will not have effect in that Contracting Party until its Office has received specified statements or documents. The U.S. made such a declaration under Article 16(2); recording of a partial change in ownership in the International Register will not have effect in the United States (37 C.F.R. 1.1065(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections under Rule 22 and effect in U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: IB may correct errors in the International Register ex officio or at the request of the holder under Rule 22; a designated Contracting Party may refuse to recognize the effects of the correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon receipt of Rule 22 corrections in a pending application, the USPTO will determine whether to give effect to the correction or refuse effects based on merits and other requirements. Corrections in abandoned applications generally will not be acted upon. U.S. patents may only be corrected under Title 35 provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence routing after transmittal
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the USPTO transmits the international design application to the International Bureau, except for matters properly before USPTO, all further correspondence concerning the application should be sent directly to the IB; replies to IB invitations must be filed directly with IB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO will generally not forward communications to the IB received after transmittal. Failure to reply directly to the IB may result in abandonment or loss of rights under Article 8. See 37 C.F.R. 1.1045(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of filing with USPTO and prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: International design applications may be filed through the USPTO via the USPTO patent electronic filing system, mail, or hand-delivery; facsimile transmission may not be used for filing an international design application or color drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants filing electronically should attach reproductions via the 'Reproductions' section of the 'Upload documents' screen rather than the generic 'Upload documents' section to avoid additional per-page publication fees required by the IB. Priority Mail Express provisions apply; Certificate of Mailing/Transmission procedures under 37 C.F.R. 1.8 do not apply to international design applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: eHague filing benefits and recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing an international design application directly with the International Bureau via WIPO’s eHague interface offers benefits including direct data entry (avoids separate DM/1 upload), real-time validation to minimize errors, automatic fee calculation, quicker IB examination, avoidance of USPTO transmittal fee, and reuse of data from previous applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using eHague also facilitates replying to WIPO communications if the application was filed through eHague. See WIPO eHague website for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO notification practices (Form PTO-2320)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO notifies applicants of receipt and transmittal (and matters preventing transmittal) via Form PTO-2320 'Notification Regarding Receipt And Transmittal Of The International Design Application To The International Bureau.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form PTO-2320 does not set a time period to cure a deficiency but warns applicants about the six-month IB-receipt window for obtaining the USPTO receipt date as the filing date. Applicants should contact USPTO before six months expire if Form PTO-2320 has not indicated transmittal.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. declaration extending refusal period and security-clearance timing (Rule 18(1)(b); Rule 13(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States declared it is extending the time period to provide a refusal to 12 months (Rule 18(1)(b)) and declared that the one-month period in Rule 13(3) shall be replaced by six months with respect to the United States due to security clearance requirements (Rule 13(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These U.S. declarations affect the timing of when an Office receipt date will count as the international filing date (IB receipt within six months) and the period for the USPTO to communicate refusals to IB (12 months). See 37 C.F.R. 1.1062(b) and related MPEP subsections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment and handling of renewal fees relative to U.S. patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment of renewal fees for international registration (Article 17 and Rule 24) is not required to maintain a U.S. patent issuing on an international design application in force; renewal fees, if required by Contracting Parties, must be submitted directly to the International Bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any renewal fee submitted to the USPTO will not be transmitted to the IB. U.S. patent term for designs is 15 years from date of grant, and renewal fees for the international registration do not affect maintenance of that U.S. patent (37 C.F.R. 1.1031(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial change in ownership recording has no U.S. effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A recording of a partial change in ownership in the International Register concerning a transfer of less than all designs shall not have effect in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. 1.1065(b) — this does not limit the owner’s right to assign or transfer a portion of interest, or to record such transfer in the Office, but recording in the International Register alone will not have U.S. effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renunciation or limitation of international registration as abandonment or amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: A renunciation of the international registration with respect to the U.S. designation will result in termination (abandonment) of a pending nonprovisional international design application; a limitation with respect to the U.S. designation will be treated as an amendment cancelling the designs subject to the limitation in the nonprovisional application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where renunciation occurs, the Office will send a notification of abandonment to the applicant or a refusal to the IB if refusal not previously communicated. Limitations are treated as cancelling designs in the U.S. prosecution record.
